prae1.title: Arriving in your body
prae1.checkin: How does your body feel right now, and how are you sleeping at the moment?
prae1.impuls:
Before we move, I'd like to tell you a little about what is happening in your body right now. Your body is producing a hormone called relaxin. It softens your ligaments and connective tissue so that your pelvis can open for the birth. That is wonderful, but it also means your joints have a little less stability. That's why we always work slowly, with control, and never to the very end of a stretch.

As your belly grows, your centre of gravity moves forward. Many women then start to arch their lower back and feel it there. At the same time your ribs widen, so that your baby has room and you can still breathe well.

And now the most beautiful part: your diaphragm, your deep abdominal muscles and your pelvic floor work together as a team. When you breathe in, the diaphragm moves down and the pelvic floor gives a little. When you breathe out, both lift again. This teamwork will stay with us through all of our sessions, before the birth and after.
ex: Come onto all fours, hands under your shoulders, knees under your hips. As you breathe in, let your breastbone move gently forward and lift your gaze a little. As you breathe out, round your back, as if you were hugging your baby with your spine. Move so slowly that your breath leads the movement.
Don't let the belly sag, keep the movement small.

Sit tall on a stable stool or the edge of your bed, feet a little wider than hip-width. Let your pelvis circle slowly, as if your tailbone were drawing a circle on the seat. Your upper body stays calm and tall. After ten circles, change direction.
It works just as well standing, with soft knees.

Stay sitting tall and reach your right arm over your head to the left. Breathe consciously into your right side, into the ribs that are opening right now. Come back as you breathe out and change sides.
Stay gentle: let your ribs widen without twisting your back.

Stand with your feet hip-width apart and spread your weight over the whole foot. Keep your knees soft and your pelvis completely neutral. Lift your breastbone a tiny bit and let your shoulders drop. Feel how your belly is carried instead of pulling you forward. From today, this is how you can stand while brushing your teeth or waiting in a queue.
Imagine a thread gently lifting you up from the crown of your head.
breath: 360° breathing

Find a comfortable seat and place your hands on the sides of your lower ribs. Breathe in through your nose and let the air flow into your hands, so your ribs widen to the sides and to the back. As you breathe out, your ribs become soft and narrow again.

We call this 360° breathing, because your ribcage opens all the way around, not only to the front. Your belly can stay soft. We breathe like this ten times: in, into your hands, then out, and let go.
med: Body scan lying on your side

Lie down on your left side with a pillow between your knees and one under your head. Your hands rest on your belly.

Move your attention slowly through your body. Feel your feet, your legs and your pelvis, which is carrying so much right now. Feel your belly under your hands, and your baby inside. Maybe your baby is moving right now, maybe they're sleeping.

Say something to your baby in your thoughts, whatever comes to you. Then take three more calm breaths in and out.
prae1.home: Five breaths of 360° breathing three times a day, for example in bed in the morning, at lunchtime and in the evening.
prae1.close: Today you laid the foundation. Everything we do in the next sessions builds on this breath.

prae2.title: Pelvic floor: engaging and letting go
prae2.checkin: Have you felt anything new since last time, maybe some downward pressure or back pain?
prae2.impuls:
Today is all about your pelvic floor. It stretches like a hammock between your pubic bone, your tailbone and your two sit bones. It is made of several layers of muscle, and right now it is carrying your organs and your baby. It keeps you continent, and it stabilises your pelvis.

Many women believe a good pelvic floor mostly has to be strong. For the birth, something else is just as important: that it can soften and open. So today we practise both, gently engaging and consciously letting go.

If you like, ask your midwife about perineal massage, which you can start from around week 34. It can help prepare the tissue for the stretch during birth.
ex: Sit tall on a chair and feel your two sit bones. Breathe in and let everything soften. As you breathe out, imagine drawing your sit bones gently towards each other and lift your pelvic floor a little inwards and upwards, as if you were picking up a blueberry. With the next breath in, let go completely. Letting go is just as important as engaging.
Glutes, thighs and belly stay relaxed, only the pelvic floor works.

Lie on your side, head resting on your arm, knees bent and heels in line with your bottom. As you breathe out, open your top knee while your feet stay together. As you breathe in, close slowly. Your pelvis doesn't roll back.
Strengthens the side of the hip that keeps your pelvis stable.
Come onto all fours and rock very gently forwards and backwards. With every breath out, feel your pelvic floor lift a little, and with every breath in, feel it widen.
Helpful if you feel downward pressure, because in this position your baby puts less weight on your pelvic floor.

Stand in front of a chair or sit on a low stool, feet wide apart and turned slightly out. Sink down low and hold on securely. Breathe into your pelvis and with every breath in let your pelvic floor become soft and wide. This is where we practise the letting go you need for the birth.
If your baby is breech after week 35 or you have symphysis pain, practise this seated only.
breath: Pelvic floor breathing

Sit comfortably or stay on all fours. Breathe in through your nose and let your belly, your ribs and your pelvic floor widen, like a flower opening. Breathe out through slightly parted lips and feel your pelvic floor lift very gently.

We take ten breaths. In and soften, out and gently lift. If you get tired, simply stay with breathing in and letting go.
med: Visualisation: opening

Lie on your side, completely comfortable with pillows. Close your eyes if you like.

Imagine a flower in a colour you love. It is still completely closed. With every breath out it opens one petal, very slowly, without you having to do anything.

Your body may open in the same way when the time comes. Not with force, but at its own pace. Stay with this flower for a few more breaths.
prae2.home: Ten breaths twice a day, letting go consciously as you breathe in.
prae2.close: If you only take one thing home today, let it be letting go as you breathe in. It will help you so much during the birth.

prae3.title: Relieving your back, strength for everyday life
prae3.checkin: How are your back and your pelvis, are there movements that hurt at the moment?
prae3.impuls:
For many women back pain is part of pregnancy, but you don't simply have to put up with it. It often comes because the belly pulls forward, the ligaments are softer and some muscles have to work harder than before. Sometimes the pain shoots down into your leg, which is called sciatica. Some women also feel pain at the front, at the pubic bone, especially on the stairs or when turning over in bed. That pain usually comes from the symphysis.

What really helps is strength. Strong legs and a strong upper back take work away from your lower back. And a few small things in everyday life make a big difference: you get up by rolling onto your side instead of pulling yourself straight up. You lift from your legs and breathe out while you do it. And when you turn over in bed, you keep your knees together.

When you sleep, lie on your side, with a pillow between your knees and a small one under your belly.
ex: Stand with your back against the wall. Your feet are hip-width apart, a little in front of you. Breathe in and slide slowly down the wall, as if you were sitting down on a chair. As you breathe out, press up through your heels. Your knees point towards your toes.
Only as deep as feels good.

Sit tall and loop the band around your feet. Hold the ends in your hands. As you breathe out, draw your elbows back and slide your shoulder blades gently towards each other. As you breathe in, let them move forward slowly. Your breastbone stays slightly lifted.
Strengthens your upper back, which helps you carry the weight of your belly and breasts.

Come onto all fours. As you breathe out, reach your right arm forward and your left leg back, only as high as your back stays calm. Come back as you breathe in. Then change sides. Imagine a cup of tea on your back that must not fall over.
With symphysis pain, lift only the arm.

Lie on your side and support yourself on your forearm, elbow under your shoulder. Your knees are bent. As you breathe out, lift your hips so that knees, hips and head form a line. Keep breathing calmly and hold. Then lower gently.
With pain at the pubic bone, leave it out and do clamshells instead.

Come into a half-kneeling position, right knee on a soft mat, left foot in front. Hold on to a chair. Gently move your pelvis forward until you feel a stretch at the front of your right hip. Breathe calmly and then change sides.
Helps counter the arched lower back that comes with a growing belly.
breath: Breathing for strength

With every strength movement, breathe out and never hold your breath. This protects your pelvic floor and your core.

Let's practise it once consciously, sitting. Breathe in and let everything widen. Breathe out and imagine you are about to lift something heavy, like a full shopping bag. Your pelvic floor lifts, your belly firms, and only then comes the movement. Ten times: in, out and lift.
med: Progressive muscle relaxation

Lie on your side, completely comfortable with pillows.

We are now going to tense individual parts of the body very lightly, one after the other, and then consciously release them. Begin with your feet: curl your toes a little, hold briefly and let go. Then your hands: make a gentle fist and let go again. Then your shoulders: draw them a little up towards your ears and let them become heavy. Finally your face: squeeze your eyes shut for a moment and let everything soften.

Notice how your body feels now. Heavier, warmer, calmer.
prae3.home: Wall squats and band rows, two sets of ten each, on three days a week.
prae3.close: Strength is not the opposite of softness. A strong body can relax so much more easily.

prae4.title: Your breath as a tool for labour
prae4.checkin: How do you feel when you think about the birth at the moment, more excited or more worried?
prae4.impuls:
Today we look at the birth, explained very simply. In the first stage the cervix opens, wave by wave. That is usually the longest stage. After that there is often a short, intense transition phase, in which many women feel they can't go on. That is a good sign, because it means it's almost time. In the pushing stage your body then actively helps to bring your baby into the world.

Maybe you know the cycle of fear, tension and pain. When we are afraid, the body tenses, and tension makes the pain stronger. Your breath is the tool you can use to break this cycle. A long, calm breath out tells your nervous system: you are safe. Then your body can release oxytocin, the hormone that makes contractions effective.

You don't have to do anything perfectly during the birth. But a breath you have practised many times beforehand will simply be there.
ex: Come onto all fours and rock forwards and backwards, then from side to side, exactly as it feels good. Breathe out long. This position takes pressure off your back during contractions.
Rest your forearms on a chair or a stack of cushions if your wrists get tired.
Kneel in front of the sofa or bed and rest your upper body on the seat or a stack of cushions. Let your pelvis circle slowly and breathe into your back. Feel how your belly is allowed to hang freely.
One of the most comfortable positions in the first stage of labour.
Hold on to a chair or a table and sink into a deep, wide squat. Let your pelvis become heavy and breathe out long.
Opens the pelvis. Not with a breech baby after week 35.
Leaning on the wall with pelvic circles
Stand with your forearms against a wall, feet hip-width apart. Let your pelvis circle slowly or swing in figures of eight, and make every breath out long, with a sound if you like.
Upright positions use gravity for your baby.
Sit on a stable stool or the edge of your bed and draw a horizontal figure of eight with your pelvis. The movement comes from the pelvis, your upper body stays calm.
Good for the mobility of the pelvis.
breath: Wave breathing and toning

You can use this breath with every contraction. Breathe in through your nose and count to four. Breathe out through your mouth and count to six or eight. The breath out is longer than the breath in, that is the secret.

Imagine every contraction is a wave. With the breath in it comes, with the long breath out you let it pass.

And now let's try toning. Breathe in, and as you breathe out let a deep sound come out, an "ooo" or an "aaah". Keep your jaw completely soft. A soft jaw also helps your pelvic floor to soften.
med: Every wave comes and goes

Lie on your side and close your eyes.

Imagine a beach. You are sitting in the warm sand, looking out at the sea. A wave comes, it grows bigger and higher, and then it breaks and ebbs away. After that it is completely calm for a while. Then the next one comes.

No wave stays forever. Every one comes and every one goes. And between the waves there is time to rest. Breathe with the waves: in as a wave comes, and a long breath out as it ebbs away.
prae4.home: Five minutes of wave breathing every day, ideally in a labour position.
prae4.close: Your breath is always with you. The more often you practise it, the more naturally it will be there during the birth.

prae5.title: Birth positions and letting go
prae5.checkin: Have you already thought about your wishes for the birth or talked to anyone about them?
prae5.impuls:
Many women only know birth from films, lying on their back. But for many it isn't the most comfortable position at all. Upright positions use gravity, give the pelvis more room and keep you mobile. During the birth you can choose any position that feels right for you, and change it at any time.

Your birth partner can help you a lot here: with a massage on your sacrum, with firm counter-pressure on your hips, with warmth on your back, and above all by reminding you to breathe when you forget. If you like, we'll practise that together today.

Write down your wishes for the birth too: which positions you'd like to try, whether you'd like music, how much light, who should take care of what. Not as a fixed plan, but so that everyone knows what feels good to you.
ex: We move slowly through the positions. Start standing, leaning against the wall, and circle your pelvis. Come into a kneeling position and rest your upper body on the sofa or a stack of cushions. Move on to all fours and rock. Finally lie down on your side, with a thick pillow between your knees. Stay in each position for a few breaths and notice which one you like best.
Write your favourite position in your workbook.
Sacral massage for your birth partner

Come onto all fours or into supported kneeling. Your birth partner places the heel of their hand flat on your sacrum, the flat area just above your bottom, and massages in slow circles. During a contraction they can press firmly and evenly. Tell them what feels good.
Practising alone: with a tennis ball against the wall.

Your birth partner stands behind you and places both palms on the sides of your hips, on the round muscles of your bottom. While you breathe out long, they gently press both sides towards each other. Many women find this a huge relief in the first stage of labour.
Only as firmly as feels good.

Sit comfortably. Briefly make fists with your hands and then let them drop completely soft into your lap. Open your mouth a little, let your lower jaw hang loose and breathe out long through your mouth. A soft mouth and soft hands help your pelvic floor to let go.
During the birth: consciously release your hands and face again and again.
breath: Breathing down

This breath is meant for the last stage of labour. Breathe in through your nose, very calmly. Breathe out slowly through your mouth and imagine your breath flowing down through your body, towards your pelvis, as if it were showing your baby the way.

Today we practise it very gently. No pushing, no holding the breath, only a long, soft breath downwards. Your pelvic floor stays wide. Ten breaths.
med: Affirmations for the birth

Lie down comfortably and close your eyes. I'm going to say a few sentences to you. Repeat them in your thoughts if they feel right for you.

My body knows what it is doing.
I open with every wave.
I trust my baby and myself.
Every contraction brings me closer to my child.
I am allowed to ask for help.

Choose the one sentence that touched you most, and breathe with it a few more times.
prae5.home: Write down your favourite affirmation and hang it where you'll see it, for example on the mirror.
prae5.close: You don't have to achieve anything during the birth. You are allowed to be guided, by your body and by your baby.

prae6.title: Preparing for the postpartum weeks
prae6.checkin: How are you feeling so close to the birth, in your body and in your thoughts?
prae6.impuls:
Today is our last session before the birth, and we are already looking a little further ahead: to the postpartum weeks. These are the first six to eight weeks after the birth. During this time your body heals a large wound inside your uterus, your pelvic floor and your core recover, and your hormones change completely.

A lovely rule of thumb is: five days in the bed, five days on the bed, five days around the bed. You are allowed to rest, get to know your baby and be cared for. Organise help now: who cooks, who shops, who looks after the older siblings.

And one more thing is important to me: in the first days after the birth many women are very tearful and sensitive. That is the baby blues, it is common and usually passes after a few days. But if the sadness stays longer than two weeks, if you feel empty or can't feel any joy with your baby, that is not weakness. Please talk to your midwife or your doctor. Postnatal depression is very treatable.
ex: Getting up by rolling to the side

Lie on your back with your knees bent. Roll onto your side in one piece, keeping your knees together. Push yourself up into sitting with both hands while your legs slide over the edge of the bed. Breathe out as you do it. This protects your core after the birth, especially after a caesarean.
After the birth, get up like this every day.
Now let's go through your favourite exercises from our sessions once more, very calmly: Cat-Cow, seated pelvic circles, wall squats and band rows. You can do this sequence every day until the birth.
Write the sequence down in your workbook.
Lie on your left side, a pillow between your knees, one under your belly and one behind your back. Let your whole body become heavy. This is also a good breastfeeding position for the first days.
In the postpartum weeks, resting is training.
breath: Emergency breath

This breath is for every moment when it all gets too much, during the birth and afterwards too, when your baby is crying and you are tired.

Breathe in through your nose and count to four. Breathe out through your mouth and count to six. Place one hand on your heart as you do it. Even three of these breaths are enough to calm your nervous system. Let's do ten now.
med: Yoga Nidra journey

Lie down completely comfortably on your side. You don't have to do anything now. You don't even have to stay awake.

I'll name places in your body one after the other, and you simply let your attention travel there. Your right thumb, your index finger, your middle finger. Your right hand, your arm, your shoulder. Your left thumb, your left hand, your arm, your shoulder. Your face, your forehead, your eyes. Your belly and your baby inside. Your pelvis, your legs, your feet.

Your whole body. It has done so much in the last months. Stay a moment longer in this stillness.
prae6.home: Write a postpartum list: who helps with what, and what do I need for myself? And send me a message when your baby has arrived.
prae6.close: I'm so looking forward to hearing from you when your baby is here. Just send me a message, and we'll plan, without any rush, when to carry on.

post1.title: Arriving after the birth
post1.checkin: How are you and your baby, and how was the birth for you? Tell me as much as you like.
post1.impuls:
Today is all about you. Every birth is different, and sometimes your own story simply needs a place where it can be told.

Your body is healing in many places at the same time right now. Your uterus is shrinking back, your pelvic floor has stretched a long way and is slowly finding its way back, and your midline also needs time to close. On top of that come the hormones and the lack of sleep. It is completely normal that your body feels unfamiliar right now.

That's why we start very gently. I'd like to ask you a few things so that I can support you well: do you sometimes leak urine when you cough, laugh or sneeze? Do you feel any downward pressure, as if something might slip out? How is your scar, if you have one? And do you have pain anywhere? Everything you tell me helps me adapt the sessions to you.
ex: Pelvic tilts lying on your back

Lie on your back with your feet hip-width apart. As you breathe out, tilt your pelvis very gently backwards so that your lower back comes closer to the mat. As you breathe in, come back. The movement is small and calm.
After a caesarean, only as long as your scar feels good.

Stay on your back with one hand on your lower belly. Breathe in and let your belly soften. As you breathe out, draw your pelvic floor gently inwards and upwards and feel your lower belly come along a little, very lightly, like a whisper.
The foundation for all further exercises.

Stay lying on your back with your knees bent. Place your fingertips across the middle of your belly, just above your navel. As you breathe out, lift your head very slightly. Feel how many fingers fit between your two long abdominal muscles and how firm or soft it feels deep down. Repeat at the level of your navel and just below.
Write width and tension in your workbook, we'll compare later.
Arm circles lying on your side

Lie on your side and draw large, slow circles with your top arm, as if you were painting a circle on the ceiling. Follow your hand with your eyes. This opens your chest and shoulders, which are tired from feeding and carrying.
breath: Breathing with pelvic floor connection

Place one hand on your heart and one on your lower belly. Breathe in through your nose, let your belly soften and your ribs widen. Breathe out through your mouth and imagine gently closing a zip from your pelvic floor up to your navel.

Not hard, just a light drawing together. Then let go again as you breathe in. Ten breaths.
med: I have arrived

Stay lying down and close your eyes. Feel the floor beneath you, carrying you.

Your body has brought a child into the world. Whatever happened during the birth, you are here and your baby is here.

Say to yourself in your thoughts: I have arrived. I am allowed to take my time. My body has done so much, and I thank it.

Stay in this feeling for a moment longer.
post1.home: Five connected breaths twice a day, ideally while feeding.
post1.close: Thank you for sharing your story with me. From now on we rebuild strength step by step, at your pace.

post2.title: Feeling your pelvic floor again
post2.checkin: How is your pelvic floor, can you feel it clearly again?
post2.impuls:
During the birth your pelvic floor stretched many times over. Afterwards it needs time and targeted training to become strong again. By the way, that is also true after a caesarean, because the pregnancy itself put pressure on it for nine months.

In everyday life you can protect it with a few simple habits. You get up by rolling onto your side. Before you cough or sneeze, you engage it briefly, this is called the Knack. And when you lift something, your baby, the car seat or the laundry basket, you breathe out first and only then lift.

If after a few weeks you still leak urine, feel downward pressure or have pain during sex, please get checked by a pelvic floor physiotherapist. That is not a small thing, and it can be treated very well.
ex: Sit tall. Engage your pelvic floor quickly and strongly for one second, and then let go completely for two seconds. You need these fast fibres when you cough, sneeze or laugh.
Letting go is just as important as engaging.
Now engage your pelvic floor slowly, inwards and upwards, and hold the tension while you keep breathing calmly. Count to five, to ten if you can. Then let go very slowly and rest for just as long.
Don't hold your breath, keep breathing calmly.

Lie on your back with your feet hip-width apart. As you breathe out, first lift your pelvic floor, then roll your pelvis up, vertebra by vertebra. As you breathe in, roll back down and release your pelvic floor.
Strengthens glutes, pelvic floor and hamstrings.
Lie on your side with your knees bent. As you breathe out, lift your pelvic floor and open your top knee while your feet stay together. As you breathe in, close slowly.
breath: The Knack

Now we practise the most important habit for your everyday life. Breathe in. Breathe out, engage your pelvic floor and then cough briefly. Feel how your pelvic floor holds you.

Now the same with lifting: breathe in, breathe out, engage and lift an object next to you, for example a cushion. First the tension, then the movement. Practise five times, until it feels natural.
med: Compassion for your own body

Lie down and place one hand on your lower belly.

Maybe you are impatient with your body right now, maybe it feels unfamiliar. That is all right. Imagine your best friend had just had a baby. How would you speak to her? You may speak to yourself just as kindly now.

Say to yourself in your thoughts: I'm giving you time. I'm patient with you. You're doing well.
post2.home: Ten quick and five long contractions three times a day, for example while feeding or at a red light.
post2.close: Your pelvic floor is a muscle like any other. With a few minutes a day it becomes strong again.

post3.title: Deep core muscles and diastasis recti
post3.checkin: How does your belly feel right now, have you done the self-check again?
post3.impuls:
During pregnancy the two long abdominal muscles that run down the front of your belly move apart to make room for your baby. This is called diastasis recti, and at the end of pregnancy almost every woman has it. For many it closes by itself after the birth, for some it needs training.

More important than the width in fingers is the tension deep down. When the midline feels firm, it can transfer force, even if two fingers still fit in between. So our goal is not only to close the gap, but to make your core strong and able to take load again.

During every exercise, watch for one sign: if the middle of your belly bulges upwards like a little tent or a ridge, this is called coning, then the exercise is still too hard for now. Make it smaller. We leave out classic sit-ups and crunches for the time being.
ex: Lie on your back with your knees bent. Breathe in and let your belly soften. Breathe out and draw your navel gently towards your spine, as if you were tightening a belt by one notch. Your pelvic floor lifts with it. Hold briefly and let go.
Your back stays still on the mat.
Stay on your back. As you breathe out, activate your core and slowly slide one heel along the floor until the leg is almost straight. As you breathe in, draw it back in. Then the other side.
It's easier in socks on a smooth floor.

On your back, lift both legs one after the other into tabletop, knees above your hips. As you breathe out, lower one foot and tap the floor with your toes. As you breathe in, come back. Your lower back stays still.
Too hard? Keep one foot on the floor.

Stay in tabletop and reach your arms up to the ceiling. As you breathe out, move your right arm back and your left leg forward, only as far as your belly stays flat. Come back as you breathe in, then the other side.
Watch for coning, and if you see it, make the movement smaller.
Come onto all fours. Breathe in and let your belly hang towards the floor. Breathe out and draw it gently inwards and upwards, without rounding your back.
Gravity makes the exercise a little more demanding here.
breath: Zip-up breathing

Lie on your back with your hands on your belly. Breathe in and let your belly widen. Breathe out slowly and imagine a zip being closed slowly from your pubic bone up to your breastbone. First your pelvic floor lifts, then your lower belly flattens, then your midline closes all the way up to your ribs.

As you breathe in, open the zip again. Ten breaths.
med: Relaxation lying on your back

Place a pillow under your knees and let your legs become completely heavy. Your arms rest loosely beside you, palms facing up.

Feel your belly rising and falling with every breath. It carried your baby and may now heal in peace. With every breath out your body sinks a little deeper into the floor. Stay like this as long as you like.
post3.home: Heel slides and toe taps, two sets of ten each, on four days a week.
post3.close: Your core needs patience, not hardness. Every calm repetition takes you further.

post4.title: Posture, carrying and feeding
post4.checkin: Where do you feel the carrying and feeding most at the moment, in your neck, your shoulders or your back?
post4.impuls:
You carry your baby, you breastfeed or bottle-feed, you lean over the changing table and lift the car seat. No wonder your neck and shoulders get tense and your upper back rounds.

When feeding, it helps to bring the baby to you, not you to the baby. A nursing pillow, a cushion under your arm and a footrest make a big difference. Your shoulders can drop and your back is supported.

When lifting, you bend your knees, hold the baby or the car seat close to your body and breathe out while you come up. Push the pram standing tall, with the handle at about hip height.

Today we strengthen your upper back and open your chest, so that your body can carry all this work more easily.
ex: Lie on your side with your knees bent and stacked, arms long in front of you. As you breathe in, open your top arm like a book to the other side and follow it with your eyes. Your knees stay together. As you breathe out, close the book again.
Opens your upper spine, which tends to round from feeding.

Sit tall with the band around your feet. As you breathe out, draw your elbows back and slide your shoulder blades together and down, away from your ears. As you breathe in, let them move forward slowly.
Without a band: bent-over row standing, with two water bottles.
Stand in a doorway and place your forearm against the frame at shoulder height. Take a small step forward until you feel a stretch at the front of your chest. Breathe calmly and change sides.
Stand hip-width apart and hold your baby or a weight close in front of your chest. As you breathe in, sit back and down, as you breathe out, lift your pelvic floor and come up through your heels.
This is exactly how you lift in everyday life.

Stand with your back against the wall, feet a little in front of it. Place your arms and the backs of your hands against the wall in a U shape. As you breathe in, slide your arms slowly up, and as you breathe out back down, your shoulders stay away from your ears.
Only as far as your arms can stay on the wall.
breath: Releasing the shoulders

Sit comfortably. Breathe in and draw your shoulders up to your ears. Hold briefly. Breathe out audibly through your mouth and let your shoulders drop down heavily.

We do this five times. Then breathe calmly five more times and feel how much space there is now between your shoulders and your ears.
med: The five-minute pause

You can take this little pause anywhere, on the sofa, while feeding or while your baby sleeps.

Close your eyes or lower your gaze. First feel your feet on the floor. Then your breath, without changing it. Then your shoulders, and let them drop a little. Then your face, your forehead, your jaw, and let everything soften.

Say to yourself in your thoughts: I am allowed to be with myself for a moment now. Stay for a few breaths, then slowly open your eyes.
post4.home: After feeding, a doorway chest stretch and ten shoulder rolls.
post4.close: You carry so much, quite literally. A strong upper back makes all of it a little easier.

post5.title: Strength for everyday life with your baby
post5.checkin: How do you feel in your body, already stronger than a few weeks ago?
post5.impuls:
Today we go one step further and build real strength. Your everyday life with a baby is physically demanding, and your body should be ready for it.

What matters is increasing the load slowly and listening to your body. There are a few warning signs that tell you an exercise is still too much for now: if you feel downward pressure, if you leak urine, if your midline bulges like a tent or if something hurts. Then you take one step back, make the exercise easier or do fewer repetitions.

That is not a step backwards. That is smart training, and that is exactly how you become strong in the long run.
ex: Stand hip-width apart, arms in front of you. As you breathe in, sit back and down, as if you were sitting onto a chair. As you breathe out, lift your pelvic floor and press up through your heels.
Progression: with your baby in your arms or a weight.
Hold on to the back of a chair. Take a big step back with your right leg and lower your knee towards the floor. As you breathe out, come back through your front heel. Then the other side.
Your front knee stays above your foot.

Lie on your back with your feet on the floor. Stretch one leg out long. As you breathe out, lift your pelvic floor and press up through the heel on the floor. Your pelvis stays level. As you breathe in, lower down.
Too hard? Start with both feet down.
Lie on your side, support yourself on your forearm, knees bent. As you breathe out, lift your hips until knees, hips and head form a line. Keep breathing calmly and hold.
Fix the band to a door handle or loop it around your feet. As you breathe out, draw your elbows back and your shoulder blades together. As you breathe in, let them move forward slowly.
Shoulders stay away from your ears.
breath: Breathing under effort

In every strength exercise: breathe out on the effort, breathe in on the release. Let's practise it standing with one squat.

Breathe in and sit back and down. Breathe out, lift your pelvic floor and come up. Feel how your whole body connects in this moment. Five repetitions, very consciously with your breath.
med: I am strong and I am held

Lie down and let your body become heavy after the training.

Feel your heart still beating a little faster and slowly becoming calmer. Feel the warmth in your muscles. Your body is strong. It carried a child, gave birth, and now it carries your child every single day.

And at the same time you are allowed to be held, by the floor beneath you, by the people around you. Say to yourself: I am strong, and I am held.
post5.home: A ten-minute strength routine with squats, glute bridges and rows, three times a week.
post5.close: You have already become so much stronger. Keep going, with patience and with joy.

post6.title: Nervous system, sleep deprivation and mental load
post6.checkin: How are you sleeping at the moment, and how are you doing with everything you have to keep in your head?
post6.impuls:
Today we do something very calm, because today is about your nervous system. Lack of sleep, the hormonal changes and the constant responsibility for a tiny human being push many mothers to their limits. You are not weak if you feel exhausted. You are human.

On top of that comes the mental load: thinking of everything, planning everything, keeping track of everything. This work is invisible, but it takes a lot of energy. A first step is to make it visible. Write down everything you think about, and share the list with your partner.

And because it matters to me, once more: if you feel empty, hopeless or cut off for a longer period, please talk to your midwife or your doctor. Postnatal depression can also begin months after the birth, and it is very treatable.

Self-care, by the way, doesn't have to take long. Even three minutes can calm your nervous system.
ex: Stand and start shaking your hands, then your arms, your shoulders, your legs, until your whole body is shaking loosely. Feel free to let a sound out. Then stand completely still and notice how you feel.
Stand hip-width apart and shift your weight gently from one leg to the other, just as you do with your baby in your arms. Let your arms swing loosely with you. This swaying calms you too.
Sit comfortably. Let your head sink slowly towards your right shoulder, breathe, and then to the left. Roll your shoulders slowly backwards. Everything very gently, without pressure.
Come onto all fours and sit back towards your heels, knees a little apart. Rest your forehead on your hands or a cushion. Breathe into your back.
Put a cushion between your bottom and heels if your knees feel strained.
Lie down with your bottom close to a wall and rest your legs up the wall. Your arms lie loosely beside you. Let the floor carry you.
breath: Long exhale and humming breath (Bhramari)

Sit comfortably or stay lying down. Breathe in through your nose and count to four. Breathe out through your nose and hum softly, like a bee, as long as it feels comfortable.

Feel how the humming vibrates in your head and in your chest. This vibration calms your nervous system especially quickly. We hum ten times. You can do this with your baby in your arms too, many babies love it.
med: Yoga Nidra

Lie down completely comfortably, cover yourself if you like. For the next few minutes you don't have to do anything at all. If you fall asleep, that's all right.

First choose a small sentence for yourself, a wish, for example: I am enough. Say it to yourself three times in your thoughts.

Now I'll travel with you through your body. Your right hand, every single finger, your wrist, your forearm, your elbow, your shoulder. Your left hand, every finger, your arm, your shoulder. Your right foot, your toes, your heel, your leg. Your left foot, your toes, your leg. Your pelvis, your belly, your back. Your chest, your throat, your face.

Your whole body is lying here now, heavy and calm.

Imagine a place where you feel completely safe. Look around there, listen to what there is to hear, feel the air on your skin.

At the end, come back to your sentence once more and say it to yourself three times. Then slowly move your fingers and toes and come back at your own pace.
post6.home: A three-minute mini break with humming breath every day.
post6.close: You are allowed to take breaks without earning them. They are simply part of it.

post7.title: Back to the movement you love
post7.checkin: Which movement do you miss most, and what are you looking forward to?
post7.impuls:
Many women ask me when they can run, jump or go back to their sport. The honest answer is: it depends less on the weeks and more on what your body can already do.

As a rough guide, running and jumping usually make sense from around twelve weeks after the birth at the earliest, and only if you have no symptoms. So no leaking, no downward pressure, no pain.

That's why today we do a load check. It is not a test you have to pass. It simply shows us where you are right now and what the next step is for you. If an exercise isn't possible without symptoms yet, that is valuable information, not a defeat.
ex: Stand on one leg with the other knee slightly lifted. Keep your balance, breathe calmly and feel your pelvic floor.
If this feels steady, that's a good sign.
Stand on one leg in front of a chair and sit down slowly, then come back up on one leg. Your knee stays above your foot.
Hold on to something if you feel unsteady.
Stand on one leg, hold the wall lightly and lift your heel as high as you can, then lower slowly.
March briskly on the spot and swing your arms. Notice whether you feel any downward pressure.
No symptoms: move on to hopping.
Hop very lightly on both feet on the spot, knees soft. If you engage your pelvic floor first and stay dry, your body is ready for the next step.
If you leak or feel pressure, stop straight away and note it in your workbook.
To finish we connect everything: squat, reverse lunge, Bird Dog and side plank, completely in the rhythm of your breath.
The sequence is in your workbook.
breath: Breathing in rhythm

When you move more again, your breath can find a rhythm. Walk slowly on the spot and breathe in for two steps and out for three steps. The breath out is a little longer.

When that feels easy, try three steps in and four steps out. Feel how your breath carries your movement.
med: The movement you love

Lie down and close your eyes.

Imagine it is a few months later. You are doing the movement you love, maybe you're running through the forest, maybe you're dancing, maybe you're standing on a mountain top. Your body feels strong and free.

How does that feel? What do you hear, what do you see? Take this picture with you, as something to look forward to and as a goal.
post7.home: Twice a week, 20 minutes of brisk walking with the pram.
post7.close: You're well on your way back to the movement you love.

post8.title: Your programme for home
post8.checkin: When you think back to our first session, what has changed since then?
post8.impuls:
Today is our last session together, and I'd like to look back with you. In the last weeks you have done so much for yourself, alongside everything a life with a baby asks of you.

What are you proud of? What can you do today that you couldn't do at the beginning? And what are you taking with you?

So that you can keep going, today we'll put together your very own programme for home. Fifteen minutes that you can do three times a week, with the exercises that did you the most good. You'll find it in your workbook afterwards too.
ex: Begin every workout with five breaths with pelvic floor connection: breathe in and soften, breathe out and gently lift.
On all fours, round and lengthen your back with your breath.
Whichever works well for you right now. Keep your midline flat.
As you breathe out, lift your pelvic floor and roll your pelvis up.
With your baby or a weight, breathe out as you come up.
On your knees or with straight legs.
breath: Your favourite breath

Which breath did you love most in our sessions? 360° breathing, wave breathing, humming breath or zip-up breathing?

Let's do it together once more now, for ten breaths. And then choose a fixed moment in your day when you'll do it from now on, for example in the morning before you get up, or in the evening when your baby has fallen asleep.
med: Closing ritual

Lie down and place both hands on your belly.

Think of the woman you were when we met. Think of everything that has happened since. The birth, the first nights, every small step back into your body.

Say to yourself in your thoughts: I am back with myself. I am strong, I am soft, and I am enough.

Take three more deep breaths in and out. Thank you for letting me walk this path with you.
post8.home: Your fifteen-minute programme, three times a week.
post8.close: It has been a real joy to work with you. If you like, I'd be so grateful for a short Google review, so that other women can find their way to me too.
